topic: dyeing and saddle stitching a vegetable tanned bridle strap that took the colour unevenly

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-2)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: waga elektroniczna do mieszania barwnika

base: I am making a bridle from vegetable tanned leather and hand stitching every strap myself.
A practice offcut from the same hide sits on the bench for testing dyes and stitches.
A digital scale stands beside it, since I mix my own dye from powder and water.
The bridle strap took the dye unevenly and shows dark clouds along one whole edge.
Should I strip the colour back and start again, or work over it with more coats?
Work over it, because stripping vegetable tanned leather usually leaves worse marks than the blotching.
Uneven colour nearly always comes from uneven wetting rather than from the dye itself.
Damp the whole strap evenly first, then flood the dye on with a wool dauber.
Several thin coats will even out a cloudy first attempt far better than one heavy one.
I dampened the strap and laid on three thin coats, which evened the colour considerably.
The clouds have gone, though the leather now feels stiffer and slightly dry to the hand.
I weighed the dye and water on the digital scale and kept the mixture exactly as before.
The practice offcut went the same way, so it is not just the bridle strap.
Is that stiffness permanent, or does it come out again once the leather is finished?
It comes out again, because the spirit in the dye has simply dried the fibres.
Rub in a light coat of neatsfoot oil and leave the strap overnight to spread.
Oil sparingly, since too much darkens the leather badly and never comes back out.
Finish with a wax the following day, once the oil has moved right through the thickness.
The oil brought the strap back to life and it drapes properly over my hand now.
I have started the saddle stitching and the first six inches look reasonably even.
Further along the stitches begin to slant differently and the back side looks untidy.
Am I pulling the two threads in the wrong order, or is the awl at fault?
Slanting stitches on the back usually mean the awl is turning slightly in your hand.
Keep the blade at a constant angle and let the diamond point mark the direction.
Always pass the same needle through first, because swapping the order twists the whole line.
Work with the strap clamped upright so both hands can move without shifting the leather.
I clamped the strap upright and kept the awl steady, which tidied the back considerably.
The stitching now runs evenly, though the thread frays badly near the end of a run.
I am using linen thread with a little beeswax rubbed along its whole length.
Should I wax it more heavily, or is the eye of the needle cutting the fibres?
The needle eye is cutting it, which happens once the thread has passed too often.
Cut shorter lengths, because a long thread rubs through the same holes many extra times.
Two arm spans is plenty for most work, however tempting a longer piece looks.
Rewax after every dozen stitches and the fraying will then stop almost entirely.
Shorter threads solved it and the whole bridle is now stitched from end to end.
The buckle billets look slightly thicker than the rest, which bothers me a little.
I skived them by hand and clearly took less off the second one than the first.
Is that worth correcting now, or will the leather settle once the bridle is used?
Correct it now, since a thick billet wears the buckle hole into an oval shape.
Skive the second one down to match, working from the flesh side with a sharp knife.
Then burnish both edges again, because skiving always leaves the edge a little ragged.
After that the bridle needs nothing but oil once a year and honest daily use.
